abstract: Automated cell tracking is widely used to quantify cellular behavior and typically involves two steps: identifying cells in each observation and linking corresponding cells across observations. This paper focuses on the linking problem under low-frame-rate imaging. Low-frame-rate imaging mitigates photobleaching and phototoxicity and enables long term observations, but larger cell displacements make spatial proximity less reliable and increase ambiguity among candidate links. We investigate whether cell images contain information about future movement direction that can provide an additional cue for cell linking. We systematically evaluate the impact of image-patch configurations, direction representations, and deep-learning architectures for movement-direction prediction accuracy. Moreover, we incorporate the predicted directions into a Linear Assignment Problem (LAP)-based linking method and evaluate linking performance across four cell lines and multiple temporal gaps. Our results show that movement-direction information can improve cell linking by 2.7 to 5.7 percentage points over the distance-only LAP baseline, depending on the cell line, at a two-hour interval between frames. Among the evaluated configurations, a CNN-LSTM with a class-based direction representation provides the largest improvement (4.1 percentage points on average) over the distance-only LAP baseline. These results show that cell images provide a cue for cell linking that spatial proximity alone does not capture.
